Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
ruminate about how to get even with assailant

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense shame
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
There is something wrong with me as a person
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

vignette: Ana's eyes would often glaze over when she tried to recount that night, the words getting stuck in her throat like a lump of unshed tears. "I just can't explain it," she'd say, frustration and shame etched on her face. The memories lingered, fragmented and disjointed, refusing to coalesce into a coherent narrative. She couldn't shake off the feeling that her body was still responding to the assault, as if danger lurked around every corner, even in the safety of her own home. As the hotel manager, Ana had always taken pride in being efficient and composed under pressure. But after the assault, she found herself working excessively long hours, using the demands of her job as a distraction from the memories that haunted her. She convinced herself that if she just kept busy enough, she wouldn't have to think about it – but the exhaustion only seemed to exacerbate the sense of being on edge all the time. Her partner, Carlos, would try to reassure her that she was safe now, but Ana couldn't shake off the feeling that there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that she was defective in some way. When memories did surface, they were often accompanied by an overwhelming sense of shame and self-blame. "I should have fought back harder," she'd tell herself, or "This happened to me because I'm not a good person." These thoughts would send her spiraling into rumination about how to get even with her assailant – fantasies of revenge that left her feeling both empowered and guilty. Ana's avoidance behaviors had become second nature. She avoided social gatherings where she might run into people who looked similar to her assailant, or anyone who might ask too many questions. Her coworkers began to notice the change in her, but Ana just attributed it to stress from work – which wasn't entirely untrue. The overwork was taking a toll on her relationships, including with Carlos, who felt like he was losing the person he loved. One day, while reviewing security footage for an incident at the hotel, Ana caught a glimpse of someone in the background who bore a striking resemblance to her assailant. Her heart racing, she quickly excused herself and spent the rest of the afternoon holed up in her office, unable to shake off the feeling of being back in that moment. She couldn't remember exactly what had happened that night – only flashes of fear and pain – but the memories seemed more real than ever. Ana knew she needed help when she realized that the avoidance behaviors weren't working anymore. The nightmares were getting worse, and even the thought of going to work filled her with dread. What finally brought her to seek therapy was the realization that she didn't have to live like this – trapped in a cycle of shame, fear, and self-blame. With Carlos's support, Ana took the first tentative steps towards confronting the memories and emotions she'd been trying to outrun for so long. As she sat in the therapist's office, Ana's eyes began to well up with tears as she whispered, "I just want to be able to tell my story without feeling like I'm going to break." The silence that followed was a fragile beginning – a chance for Ana to reclaim her narrative and start rebuilding herself, one small step at a time.
